## ncomms10369-s1.pdf  [other]
[S1] Supplementary Figure 1. [S2] ​ Two groups of responders to the HBV vaccine can be identified based on the antibody response titers (a) Response plots showing antibody titers as function of the vaccination status (x­axis: before and after receiving the vaccines). [S3] The analysis was restricted to subjects with undetectable titers pre­vaccination (hep. [S4] B: n= 170, dip: n=105, tet: n=67 and chol: n=151). [S5] The titers for HBsAg (hep. [S6] B), diphtheria toxin (dip.), tetanus toxin (tet.) and cholera toxin (chol.) are given on natural log scale. [S7] The unit of every titer is given in the y­axis label. [S8] Red horizontal lines indicated standard titer cutoffs used to define protective antibody levels. [S9] The percentage of patients having antibody titers above the protective thresholds (Protect. [S10] Ab) post­vaccination is indicated above each plot. [S11] (b) Density of the anti­HBsAg levels detected post­vaccination. [S12] Ab titers are given in mIU/mL in natural log scale space. [S13] 94 of the 174 subjects (54%) present Ab titers below the detection threshold of 5 mIU/mL while 79 subjects presented Ab titers ranging between 5.07 to 17,311.4 mIU/mL. [S14] Kernel density estimation of the Ab titers revealed two groups of responders based on Ab titers, HBV vaccine poor­responders (red line) with Ab titers below the detection threshold and HBV vaccine responders (black line) with Ab titers above 5 mIU/mL. [S15] Supplementary Figure 2.​ ​ Development of the BioAge signature on the SAFHS cohort (a) Scatter plot showing the gap statistic estimation of the optimal number of cluster of genes among the 2285 genes correlated to age on the SAFHS cohort. [S16] The x­axis corresponds to the different number of clusters tested and the y­axis corresponds to the gap statistic (Gap) and its 95% confidence interval. [S17] The gap statistic corresponds to the between­clusters variance divided by the intra­cluster variance (the greater the gap statistic the better the fit). [S18] The optimal number of clusters was obtained following the rule described in Tibshirani ​ et al. [S19] defined as the smallest k such that Gap(k) ≥Gap(k+1) – sd(k+1). [S20] Consequently, twenty clusters were identified as the optimal number of clusters of genes. [S21] (b) Scatter plot showing the chronological age as a function of the BioAge on the SAFHS dataset. [S22] Among the 109 donors aged 65 or over (which is the population with the same age range as the elderly in EM131), 42 (39%) have a young BioAge (BioAge < 0) while 67 (61%) have an old BioAge (BioAge ≥ 0). [S23] Supplementary Figure 3. [S24] Boxplot showing the BioAge score as a function of HBV vaccine response on the EM131 elderly cohort A Wilcoxon rank­sum test was used to test for statistical difference in BioAge between HBV vaccine responders (R) and poor­responders (PR), the ​ p​ ­value is presented above the boxplot. [S25] Supplementary Figure 4. [S26] Scatter plot showing the results of the 10­fold cross­validation on the EM131 training set. [S27] The red line corresponds to naïve Bayes classifier of 15 genes, which gave an estimated accuracy of 62.6% accuracy. [S28] Supplementary Figure 5. [S29] FCM and cytokines associated with response to the HBV vaccine on the EM131 training set (a) Examples of our gating procedure for obtaining the percentage of memory IgG+ B cell populations (CD3­CD19+HLA­DR+CD20+CD27+CD10­IgG+) among total B cells (CD3­CD19+HLA­DR+) for subject 2087 at visit 2 (value=12.6%). [S30] Please see Supplementary Table 5a for cell population annotations. [S31] (b­c) Cytokine­expression was analyzed in order to identify markers of response to the HBV vaccine. [S32] (b) Boxplots presenting the levels of three cytokines selected in the forward selection model between responders and poor­responders to the HBV vaccine on the EM131 training set. [S33] The three cytokines selected are implicated in the inflammatory mechanism. [S34] (c) ROC curves for the prediction of the HBV vaccine response using the cytokine data on the EM131 test set. [S35] Supplementary Figure 6. [S36] Integrative analysis reveals negative correlations between biomarkers of response and hyporesponse to the HBV vaccine (a) ​ EIF2 signaling pathway is associated with hyporesponse to the HBV vaccine​ . [S37] Ingenuity EIF2 canonical pathway where nodes are colored by the fold­change difference between HBV vaccine responders (R) compared to poor­responders (PR) as calculated on the EM131 training set. [S38] (b) Least square regressions between pairs of “omics” was performed using the R package “mixOmics”. [S39] The results regression coefficients were converted to Pearson correlation between pairs of features of the different “omics”. [S40] Significant (​ t​ ­test: ​ p ≤0.05) negatives correlations are presented as edges and the features as vertices. [S41] The vertices are colored by fold­change between HBV vaccine responders vs. [S42] poor­responders of the EM131 training set. [S43] Supplementary Figure 7. [S44] Proposed mechanism leading to hyporesponse to HBV vaccine Hypoxia (HIF­1α signaling pathway) leads to the increase in red blood cells. [S45] Turnover of red blood cells will release free­hemoglobin in the circulation. [S46] Hemoglobin, a source of heme­complex, will trigger the activation of the heme­regulated eIF2α kinase (HRI), In turn, HRI will stimulate the production of type I interferon by pDCs and promote the release of pro­inflammatory cytokines in the system. [S47] The resulting inflammatory response will hinder response to HBV vaccination. [S48] A negative feedback loop involving haptoglobin (HP) and CD163 will be activated to catalyze the degradation of cell­free hemoglobin. [S49] In parallel, the absence of B­cell activation or the low frequency of memory B­cell will result in hyporesponse to HBV vaccine. [S50] The datasets (transcriptomic, FCM, cytokines/chemokines and hematologic) supporting the elements of the proposed mechanism are indicated on the figure. [S51] Supplementary Table 1 ​ Clinical characteristics of the study cohort All participants were of European descent with BMI below 35 kg/m​ 2​; ~55% were women; and none had histories of autoimmunity, immunomodulating medications, cancer, recent vaccination or recent infection. [S52] The Fisher’s exact test (categorical variable) and the Wilcoxon Rank sum test (continuous variable) were used to assess difference between the EM131 training set and EM131 test set. [S53] No significant difference in term of clinical (BMI: body mass index) or serological (HepB: hepatitis B, Dip: diphtheria, Tet: tetanus) variables was observed between those two sets. [S54] Supplementary Table 2​ ​ Logistic regression with poor­response to HBV vaccination Univariate and Multivariate logistic regression against response to HBV vaccine was performed using clinical variables and the BioAge signature. [S55] Only variables presenting a significant association with response to HBV vaccine at the univariate level (z­test: ​ p​ ­value ≤0.05) were included in the multivariate level. [S56] Age, gender and the BioAge are significantly associated with HBV vaccine response in the univariate analysis. [S57] The BioAge signature maintains significant association with HBV vaccine response even after correcting for clinical variable like age and gender. [S58] Supplementary Table 3a.
